readerTitle: Why "keep the tables clean" isn't an instruction
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑 서버, 소프트웨어 개발자) + 실제 연구 (Gallup Q12 설문 첫 문항)
insight: 많은 '성과 문제'는 노력의 문제가 아니라 기대치의 차이다. 두 사람이 같은 결과물을 보고 같은 판정을 내릴 수 있을 만큼 구체적으로 말해야 기대치가 된다.
misconception: 좋은 직원이라면 말하지 않아도 무엇을 기대하는지 안다. 기대치를 구체적으로 말하는 것은 마이크로매니징이다.

sources.text: Gallup Q12 Employee Engagement Survey, item 1: "I know what is expected of me at work."
레스토랑과 개발자 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Gallup Q12의 첫 문항이 "I know what is expected of me at work"이며 Gallup이 이를 참여도의 기초 요건으로 설명한다는 점을 Gallup 공식 자료로 다시 확인하세요. 응답 비율 같은 수치는 연도마다 달라 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
"2분 안에 테이블 정리", "중급 휴대폰에서 2초 이내 로딩"은 설명용 가상 기준이며 업계 표준을 주장하지 않습니다.

cards.title: Why "keep the tables clean" isn't an instruction
body: On her first day, a manager tells a new server: "Keep the tables clean." The server nods. She works hard all night.
By the Friday rush, three empty tables sit covered in plates while guests wait at the door. The manager is annoyed. The server thinks she did exactly what she was asked.

image.label: Empty restaurant tables with dirty plates while guests wait at the door
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 바쁜 레스토랑 저녁, 앞쪽에 접시가 남은 빈 테이블 세 개, 입구에는 기다리는 손님들. 뒤편에 열심히 일하는 서버와 팔짱 낀 매니저. 실제 브랜드 로고나 간판은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What do you say to the server?
body: You're the manager. It's the middle of the rush, and you have a minute to talk to her before the next wave of guests.

options.text: "You need to pay more attention to the tables."
options.feedback: It's quick, but it repeats the same vague words more firmly. She'll try harder at her own idea of clean, and the gap stays.

options.text: "When guests leave, clear and reset the table within two minutes, even when it's busy. Let's do the next one together."
options.feedback: It takes a minute now, but she knows what done looks like, how fast, and that it matters most in a rush. You can both see if it's happening.

options.text: Say nothing now, then write a checklist of all closing duties and pin it up tomorrow
options.feedback: Written standards help later. But tonight's tables stay dirty, and a long list may still miss the one thing you care about: speed during the rush.

cards.title: Both of them were right.
body: To the manager, *clean* meant cleared, wiped and reset with cutlery soon after guests leave, so the next party can sit down.
To the server, *clean* meant wiped properly when she had a free moment. On a busy night, she had none.
She didn't lack effort or skill. The two of them had two different pictures of good work, and nobody noticed until it went wrong.

cards.title: Setting expectations
body: **Setting expectations** means describing what good work looks like before the work starts, clearly enough that someone else could check it.
A simple test: if you and your employee looked at the same result, would you both judge it the same way? If not, you've given a wish, not an expectation.

image.label: Vague instruction versus a clear expectation side by side
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 말풍선 "Keep the tables clean" 아래에 각자 다른 그림을 떠올리는 두 사람. 오른쪽 말풍선 "Reset within 2 minutes, even when busy" 아래에 같은 그림을 떠올리는 두 사람. 담백한 파스텔 톤.

cards.title: Four things a clear expectation includes.
body: Most good expectations answer four questions:
list: **Outcome:** what should be true when it's done?
**Check:** how will we both know it happened?
cards.callout: Then add the *why*. People apply a standard better when they know what it protects.
cards.softwareNote: In software teams, this is the difference between a ticket that says "improve onboarding" and one with a clear definition of done that anyone on the team could test.

cards.title: It's the first question for a reason.
body: Gallup's long-running workplace survey, the Q12, opens with one statement: "I know what is expected of me at work." Gallup treats it as a foundation. If people can't answer it, the other things a manager does matter less.
One practical habit helps: ask the person to say the expectation back in their own words. Gaps show up in seconds, not on Friday night.

cards.title: Clear isn't the same as controlling.
body: Spell out the outcome and the standard, not every step. Telling someone exactly how to hold the cloth turns an expectation into micromanaging and leaves no room for a better method.
Expectations also go stale. When priorities change, say so out loud. An old standard nobody updated is just another gap.
And keep it to what matters most. Twenty "top priorities" means none.

cards.title: Now it's a software team.
body: Customers complain your app's checkout is slow. You ask a developer to fix it. Which request sets the clearest expectation?

options.text: "Please make checkout faster, as soon as you can."
options.feedback: It's easy to say, but faster could mean a 5% gain or a full rebuild. You may get weeks of work on the wrong thing.

options.text: "Checkout should load in under 2 seconds on a mid-range phone by the end of this sprint. We'll both check it with the same test. It matters because people abandon slow carts."
options.feedback: Outcome, standard, timing, check and why are all there. The developer still chooses how to get there.

options.text: "Rewrite the image loading and remove these three scripts by Friday."
options.feedback: It's very clear, but it sets steps, not a result. If those changes don't make checkout fast, the task is done and the problem isn't.

cards.title: People can't hit a target they can't see.
body: Before judging someone's work, check whether you ever described what good looked like clearly enough to check.
**Try it today:** pick one task you hand off often. Write its outcome, standard, timing and check in four short lines. Then ask the person to say it back.
